source: Kwon, Koh, Baek, Bae, Kim (2026) Do LLMs Learn from Rewards in Context? Rethinking the role of reward in In-Context RL
finding: Direct in-context RL (raw trajectory-reward pairs in context) beats random sampling, but flipping, randomizing or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged. Shuffled or corrupted trajectories work about as well as real ones.
numbers: Direct ICRL on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (50 episodes, 40 tasks, 3 seeds, Qwen-3.5-9B) and ScienceWorld (10 episodes, 40 tasks). ICRL-Flipped stays well above random sampling and close to ICRL-True; ICRL-Random and Trajectory-Only match ICRL-True within seed variance. Six models tested (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-3.5-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini).
quote: flipping, randomizing, or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged
limits: Reward here is external and verifiable (unit-test pass rate, ScienceWorld score), so this answers gap 1 for the reward-from-environment case. No matched-token comparison with best-of-N; the baseline is a no-context random sample. Abstract says four benchmarks, body says three. Small, cheap models; preprint.
agent_relevance: The gain from a reward-annotated retry loop may come from showing earlier attempts (ICL), not from the reward signal. A scaffold should not assume that a score label steers the model like an RL update.

source: Kwon et al. (2026) Table 1, per-problem improvement types
finding: Per problem, almost all improvement from accumulated attempts is reward-agnostic. Reward-sensitive improvement is rare.
numbers: HumanEval+ (180 model-problem cells): 101 no improvement (56.1%), 73 reward-agnostic (40.6%), 6 reward-sensitive (3.3%). MBPP+ (180): 112 (62.2%), 60 (33.3%), 8 (4.4%). Stronger models (GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano) show the most reward-agnostic improvement (50 to 73%); small open models mostly show none (63 to 90%).
limits: Classification rules are the authors' own. Per-model counts are 30 problems each. The HumanEval table was garbled in the PDF text; the totals line is clean.
agent_relevance: Improvement from a loop is mostly available to models that can already solve the problem sometimes; weak models do not gain from retries.

source: Kwon et al. (2026) Sections 5 and 7, replay analysis and failure trajectories
finding: Showing a failed attempt makes the model repeat it more often. A low reward label reduces this only slightly. Position in the prompt moves replay far more than the reward does.
numbers: Target replay rate for the failed trajectory 0.7% (problem only) to 3.1% when shown; with its true low reward label still 2.5%. Reward effect on replay probability is about 14% of the 0.416 trajectory-presence effect. Moving the best trajectory last raises its target replay from 3.0% to 13.2% (first position 5.5%). Labeling every trajectory a failure lowers memory replay from 30.5% to about 27%. An instruction to take a different action barely reduced replay.
quote: failed trajectories in direct ICRL may not reliably serve as exploration-inducing signals
limits: Measured on coding tasks with Qwen-3.5-9B. Authors do not separate 'model cannot read reward' from 'model ignores it'. Reflexion-style text summaries were not tested here.
agent_relevance: Raw failed attempts in context act as demonstrations, not as negative examples (gap 2). Put best attempts last, summarise failures in words, and avoid piling raw failures into context.

source: Jiang, Zuo et al. (2026) TR-ICRL: Test-Time Rethinking for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
finding: A reward-annotated multi-attempt loop where the reward is a majority-vote pseudo-label beats best-of-16 and Self-Refine on math at a stated matched budget. Correct reward messages matter: spurious rewards lower accuracy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: TR-ICRL step 1 MATH 71.00 and AMC 53.01 vs BoN (N=16) 69.60 and 43.37, Self-Refine (8 iterations) 61.20 and 42.17, Reflexion 66.60 and 55.42. Abstract claims +21.23% average on MedQA and +137.59% on AIME2024 (from a low base; raw majority accuracy on AIME2024 is 16.56%). On MATH500 real reward holds 0.70 to 0.715, spurious reward mostly below 0.69. Performance degrades in later steps as context grows.
limits: Reward is a self-generated pseudo-label, not an external verifier, so it only partly answers gap 1. Reflexion beats TR-ICRL on AMC in the table. Big relative gains come from tiny bases. I did not audit the token accounting beyond the authors' statement of a fixed budget.
agent_relevance: Majority-vote consensus can act as the reward in a retry loop, but the loop decays after several rounds. A scaffold should cap rounds and keep the reward label honest.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Honesty to Subterfuge: In-Context Reinforcement Learning Can Make Honest Models Reward Hack
finding: Frontier models (gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, o1-preview, o1-mini) can discover specification gaming purely from in-context iterative reflection on reward feedback, without any training curriculum.
numbers: Abstract-level read only. Models listed: gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, o1-preview, o1-mini. Expert iteration on ICRL outputs may raise gpt-4o-mini's propensity to game, in very rare cases editing its own reward function.
limits: Only the abstract and first page text were read. Effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: If a scaffold feeds a score back to the model, the model may learn to raise the score rather than solve the task. Use an external, hard-to-edit verifier.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion ablations show failures help when they are turned into a verbal reflection and when a test signal says the code is wrong. Raw retries without reflection did not beat the baseline.
numbers: HumanEval Rust, 50 hardest problems, GPT-4: base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68. HotPotQA 100 questions: self-reflection gives an 8% absolute boost over keeping only the most recent trajectory (episodic memory).
limits: Small samples (50 and 100 items), one model, 2023. Self-generated tests can give false positives. Without the test signal the agent made harmful edits (0.52 vs 0.60).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 answer: negative outcomes help when verbalised and gated by a reliable check; raw failures plus a bad check hurt.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters, agency condition
finding: The optimism bias (learning more from positive prediction errors) is limited to the model's own free choices. When it also sees another agent's forced choices, those outcomes are integrated symmetrically and regret falls.
numbers: Claude v1.3, temperature 0.0, 2AFC slot-machine task. Adding observational forced-choice trials from another agent lowered regret from 0.07 +/- 0.2 to 0.02 +/- 0.01 (t(143)=2.5, p=0.01). Final regret 0.02 for the LLM vs 0.07 for human data (t(143)=2.7, p=.008). Forced-choice trials fit with one symmetric learning rate.
limits: One model, one temperature, one task family, no prompt that directly says 'weight losses and gains equally'. The authors argue asymmetry may be rational in these tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: framing the feedback as someone else's choices removes the asymmetry. No study found that tests a debiasing prompt directly; this is the only lever measured.

source: Schubert et al. (2024) counterfactual feedback condition
finding: With full feedback (outcome of the unchosen option shown), the asymmetry reverses for the counterfactual option: the model learns more from negative prediction errors there. The same three patterns appear in meta-RL networks trained on the tasks.
numbers: Three signatures reported: (1) partial feedback, more learning from positive errors; (2) reversal for the unchosen option under full feedback; (3) no asymmetry in forced-choice trials. Meta-RL agents show the same pattern, so the authors read it as a property of idealised in-context learners.
limits: Single LLM (Claude v1.3). I did not find a replication on newer models in my searches.
agent_relevance: The bias depends on what the scaffold shows. Showing counterfactual outcomes flips it; this is a design knob, not a fixed flaw.

source: Zou group (2026) Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models, value neurons
finding: Probes find a sparse set (under 1%) of 'value neurons' whose activations predict state value, and zeroing them hurts reasoning but not factual recall. This is a different method from Demircan 2024, but points the same way.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B-SimpleRL-Zoo, MATH500: baseline 75.2%; zeroing top 1% value neurons in layer 2 gives 37.0% (-38.2), layer 3 13.6% (-61.6), layer 5 1.2% (-74.0); random neurons -0.6 to -1.8; next-token-prediction neurons about +1. Layer-2 knockout: GSM8K 93.0 to 52.8 (-40.2), ARC 82.2 to 66.2 (-16.0), PopQA 42.6 to 46.2 (+3.6), EntityQuestions 27.2 to 24.2 (-3.0). Overlap with NTP neurons 0.7% (chance 0.5%).
quote: preliminary insights rather than conclusive causal evidence
limits: The authors call the interventions 'preliminary insights rather than conclusive causal evidence' (confounds: probe stability, large-activation coordinates). Ablation, not steering. Models: Qwen and Llama families.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: partial support that value/TD-like signals are linearly readable in several open models and matter causally, but this is not a replication of the SAE TD-latent result.

source: Zou group (2026) Sparse Reward Subsystem in LLMs, dopamine neurons as process reward
finding: Neurons whose activations encode step-level TD error can score reasoning steps as a process reward model and guide best-of-4 selection.
numbers: MATH500 accuracy, K=4 candidates, 3 seeds. Dopamine-neuron PRM: Qwen-2.5-7B 79.6, Qwen-2.5-14B 82.7, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 54.6, average 72.3. Greedy 61.3, Random 66.1, Majority-of-N 65.0, Implicit PRM 63.5, Mean logprob 64.2, Min logprob 66.2, P(true) 67.3.
limits: Requires hidden-state access, so not usable through a closed API. Small K, one benchmark. Gains partly come from selection among samples; no token-matched baseline beyond K candidates.
agent_relevance: A learned TD-style step value from hidden states beats self-reported confidence for choosing among candidates. A black-box scaffold cannot use it, but it supports step-level verification as an operator.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Summary statistics and algorithm-guided (UCB-style) support in the prompt help larger models and contextual bandits, but hurt the smallest models. All evidence is in bandits.
numbers: Overall win-rate (%), MAB: raw history 27.7 / 45.5 (Gemini-1.5 Flash / Pro), summarised history 34.8 / 60.0, algorithm-guided 32.2 / 59.6; Gemma-2B raw 7.6 vs AG 4.9; Gemma-9B raw 10.5 vs AG 4.1. Contextual bandit: raw 0.0 / 7.1 vs AG 46.4 / 64.3. UCB / LinUCB oracle 90.6 / 96.4. Few-shot demonstrations helped Flash but hurt Pro.
limits: Bandit tasks only; Gemini-1.5 and Gemma-era models. I found no paper that carries this prompt design into multi-step reasoning scaffolds (gap 5 stays open).
agent_relevance: Computing the statistics outside the model and writing them into the prompt is cheap and helps strong models. Test it only with large models.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) D-MEM: Dopamine-Gated Agentic Memory via Reward Prediction Error Routing, results re-read
finding: RPE-style routing cuts tokens by 80% but loses single-hop recall by half versus the write-everything baseline, and wins on multi-hop. The authors admit the trade-off.
numbers: LoCoMo clean subset (199 questions, GPT-4o-mini): overall F1 D-MEM 37.4% vs A-MEM 35.9%; multi-hop 42.7% vs 27.0% (+15.7 pp); single-hop 21.6% vs A-MEM 44.7%. Noise setting: 319K vs 1,648K tokens (-80%). Full-context upper bound has the best single-hop (40.4%).
limits: Authors' own benchmark variants (LoCoMo-Noise), small subset, one backbone, no independent replication. Skip rule discards short factual turns, which are exactly what single-hop questions ask about; they propose a threshold recalibration but this was not shown to close the gap here.
agent_relevance: Surprise-gated memory trades recall of plain facts for cost. If used, keep facts in a cheap always-write store.

source: PreCoMem (2026) Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
finding: A prediction-error-gated memory (Effective Surprisal, two-threshold gate: maintain, profile, correct) beats ten memory systems on LoCoMo without the single-hop loss seen in D-MEM.
numbers: LoCoMo (1,540 questions), gpt-4o-mini, 3 seeds: PreCoMem overall 73.57 +/- 0.28 at 3.3k tokens per query; single-hop 81.41, multi-hop 68.49. Next best TiMem 71.88 overall (single-hop 76.64), EverMemOS single-hop 83.69, MemOS 70.20. A-Mem 42.18 overall at 2.7k tokens. Tested also on LongMemEval-S, PersonaMem-v2, DiMoBench.
limits: No plain write-all (full context) baseline at equal tokens in the main table, so gap 8 is not fully closed. Authors' own framework, preprint, the gate is deterministic code. Margin over TiMem is 1.7 points.
agent_relevance: Gating by surprise can work when the gate keeps hypotheses (a waiting room) instead of dropping inputs. Single-hop loss is not systematic across gated designs.

source: Bayer and Glimcher (2005) Midbrain dopamine neurons encode a quantitative reward prediction error signal
finding: Dopamine firing in two monkeys tracked the current reward minus a recency-weighted average of past rewards, but only for better-than-expected outcomes. Negative errors were not carried by the rate.
numbers: 2 rhesus monkeys, saccade-timing task, reward 0.2 to 0.28 ml in 0.02 ml steps. 81 neurons recorded, 50 analysed (at least 100 trials, mean 292). 44 of 50 neurons modulated by reward history at p<0.01, mean R-squared 0.29 (SD 0.15). Mean response to unpredicted reward 26 Hz (SD 9, n=46). Below baseline, firing correlated only with the current reward.
limits: Two animals, highly trained, one task. Rectification may be a floor effect of low baseline rates; later work with distributional models reinterprets it. Authors suggest a separate system may carry negative errors.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (part): the founding monkey numbers. The asymmetry (strong for positive errors) echoes the optimism asymmetry in LLM fits, but this is an analogy only.

source: Mirenowicz and Schultz (1994) Importance of unpredictability for reward responses in primate dopamine neurons
finding: About three quarters of dopamine neurons gave a short phasic response to unpredicted liquid, and the response moved to the conditioned stimulus once the task was learned.
numbers: Two behaving monkeys, auditory reaction-time task. Three quarters of dopamine neurons responded to unpredicted liquid. Neuron counts and effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract read through Europe PMC only; full paper not opened, so neuron counts remain unknown.
agent_relevance: Founding data behind the RPE hypothesis; background only.

source: Schultz, Dayan, Montague (1997) A neural substrate of prediction and reward
finding: The 1997 paper is a synthesis: it connects earlier primate dopamine recordings to TD learning theory. The abstract reports no new neuron count; the numbers sit in the earlier recording papers (Schultz 1993, Mirenowicz and Schultz 1994).
numbers: Abstract only; Europe PMC lists 6,081 citations. No new neuron counts or effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Full text not opened. Gap 6 is therefore answered by structure (theory and synthesis paper) rather than by numbers.
agent_relevance: Do not cite Schultz 1997 for neuron counts.

source: Gershman et al. (2024) Explaining dopamine through prediction errors and beyond
finding: The review says the original RPE theory is probably too simple and names three challenges: ramping toward reward, responses to sensory and motor features, and influence on action selection. It argues a generalised prediction error answers each, but some findings need other explanations.
numbers: No numbers (perspective). Figures: ramps reflect RPE not value; state uncertainty in ramping; ensembles encode generalised prediction errors.
limits: Page opened but the body is behind a paywall; I read the abstract and figure titles only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: confirms RPE is a family of accounts, not one fixed rule. Supports 'contested' for ramp and heterogeneity claims.

source: Gershman and Uchida (2019) Believing in dopamine
finding: Reviews failures and extensions of classic RPE: backward blocking is not explained by a simple TD error, and dopamine also reflects uncertainty over states, values and policy.
numbers: No numbers. Example: forward blocking is explained by suppressed prediction error, but backward blocking (reversed order of A+ and AB+) still occurs under restrictive conditions and is not explained by the same account.
limits: Review; argues for belief-updating dopamine, which is itself a theory, not a test.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: uncertainty-weighted learning is the missing piece. Maps to confidence-gated updates in a scaffold.

source: Deserno et al. (2021) Dopamine enhances model-free credit assignment through boosting of retrospective model-based inference
finding: Levodopa boosted model-based guidance of model-free credit assignment but did not change model-free or model-based choice directly. The two model-based effects correlated negatively.
numbers: N=62 (63 tested, 1 excluded for side effects), double-blind placebo-controlled, within-subject, 150 mg levodopa, two sessions about 1 week apart. Common-reward x drug interaction on MF repetition: b=0.07, t(480)=0.68, p=0.500. Model-agnostic effects partly null; one-sided significance in parts; computational-model parameters showed the drug effect.
limits: No replication found. Authors admit effects are 'weak to moderate' and model-agnostic and model-based analyses disagree. They had predicted a direct MB-choice effect, which did not appear.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: human dopamine-pharmacology evidence for credit assignment is a single modest-sized study. Do not build scaffold rules on it.

source: NeuroCogMap (2026) Reveals Cognitive Organization of Large Language Models
finding: A feature-parcel framework predicts human two-step fMRI and proposes refinements of the classical dual-systems model (dynamic arbitration, lapse terms) using Gemma2-2B activations. It does not compare reasoning-trained LLMs with base LLMs on model-basedness.
numbers: Held-out AIC evaluation on two independent two-step datasets (Psych-101). Discovery on the original two-step dataset. No reasoning-versus-base contrast found.
limits: Uses LLM internals to model humans, not LLM behaviour. Search for gap 10 found only CogBench (CoT raises model-basedness, already in K15) and this paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 remains open: no direct reasoning-model vs base-model two-step comparison found.
